body.text: Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) is Canada's largest federal program supporting business R&D. Taxpayers carrying on business in Canada can deduct qualifying SR&ED expenditures under the Income Tax Act and earn investment tax credits. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations earn a 35% enhanced credit on up to $6,000,000.

This entry examines the research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework, direct innovation funding stack, provincial and territorial tax credit regimes, administrative procedures, and judicial precedents of Canada as of November 2026.

Canada's flagship innovation incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—operates through a dual-benefit statutory mechanism under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations. First, taxpayers carrying on business in Canada may pool and deduct allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) in the current taxation year or carry those undeducted pool balances forward indefinitely to reduce net income for tax purposes in future taxation years. Second, claimants earn Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) and refundable ITCs under section 127.1 on qualified SR&ED expenditures. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 prior taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset Part I tax otherwise payable.

Following the enactment of Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, Canada implemented the most significant structural expansion of the SR&ED program since 2012, applicable to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. These legislative reforms doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average annual revenue phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, at the provincial level, Québec enacted a major overhaul effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing its legacy R&D wage and university credits with the harmonized Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) at refundable rates of 30% (up to $1,000,000 above an exclusion threshold) and 20% thereafter, expanding coverage to pre-commercialization and capital property acquisitions.
Section 1: Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution of the SR&ED Regime
1.1 Historical Foundations and Statutory Authority

Canada's statutory commitment to incentivizing industrial research dates back to 1944 amendments to the Income War Tax Act, the legislative predecessor to the modern Income Tax Act, which first permitted Canadian corporations to deduct research and development outlays against business revenue despite the general capital expenditure prohibitions later codified in section 18 of the Act. The modern framework of federal SR&ED incentives has been in continuous operation since 1985 and is jointly governed by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy and approves special-purpose buildings, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical and financial compliance across the country. Each year, the SR&ED program provides more than $3 billion in tax incentives to businesses in Canada, making it the single largest federal program supporting business R&D.
The legal authority for the SR&ED program rests on four primary statutory and regulatory pillars within the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations:

items: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act: Establishes the exhaustive statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" (paragraphs (a) through (k)), which applies uniformly across the Act.

Section 37 of the Income Tax Act: Governs the computation, pooling, deductibility, and indefinite carryforward of allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada (subsection 37(1)) and permissible deductions for research conducted outside Canada (subsection 37(2)), alongside rules for traditional versus proxy elections (clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) and subsection 37(10)), specified employee bonus exclusions (subsection 37(9)), mandatory filing deadlines (subsections 37(11) and 37(11.1)), and loss restriction events (subsection 37(6.1)).

Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act: Define "qualified expenditure," "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool," "investment tax credit," "contract payment," "government assistance," "non-government assistance," "taxable supplier," "first term shared-use-equipment," "second term shared-use-equipment," and "eligible Canadian public corporation" (subsection 127(9)); establish the 15% basic and 35% enhanced ITC calculation and expenditure limits (subsections 127(5) and 127(10.1) to 127(10.8)); govern non-arm's length transfers (subsection 127(13)), unpaid amounts (subsection 127(26)), and ITC recapture (subsections 127(27) to 127(36)); and authorize cash refundability for qualifying entities (section 127.1).

Sections 2900 to 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations: Prescribe directly attributable overhead and salary expenditures under the traditional method (subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) calculation, overall proxy cap, and specified employee salary base limits (subsections 2900(4) through 2900(10)), prescribed depreciable property exclusions for shared-use equipment (subsection 2900(11)), prescribed non-qualifying expenditures (section 2902), and prescribed special-purpose buildings (section 2903).

body.text: 1.2 The 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms (Bill C-15, Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024 (following measures enacted from the 2012 Federal Budget), the federal SR&ED regime operated under restricted parameters: capital expenditures and capital lease costs were completely excluded from SR&ED incentives, the basic ITC rate stood at 15% (reduced from 20% prior to 2014), the prescribed proxy rate stood at 55% (reduced from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013), and the enhanced 35% refundable ITC was restricted exclusively to CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of qualified expenditures.

Following consultations initiated in 2024 and proposals announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025), Parliament enacted Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. To align administrative practice with Bill C-15, the CRA published revised statutory forms in May 2026 and updated core financial policies between May and October 2026.

body.text: 1.3 Status of the Proposed Patent Box Regime vs. the Productivity Mega Deduction

A frequent point of confusion in secondary tax commentary involves the status of a Canadian "Patent Box" regime. In Budget 2024, the federal government noted that its patent box consultation had closed on April 15, 2024, and indicated that submissions would inform future decisions on a preferential intellectual property (IP) income tax regime. While the 2024 Fall Economic Statement signalled that Patent Box details would follow in 2025, Budget 2025 (released November 4, 2025) omitted any Patent Box provisions. Instead, Budget 2025 prioritized the Bill C-15 SR&ED enhancements and allocated $75,000,000 for the National Research Council's (NRC) IP Assist Program and $22,500,000 for the Patent Collective.

Furthermore, neither the May 2026 Spring Economic Update nor the Department of Finance's 2026 pre-budget consultations (which ran from July 6, 2026, to September 8, 2026) included a Patent Box proposal. On September 15, 2026 (with formal draft legislation released on October 1, 2026), the federal government unveiled the Productivity Mega Deduction, expanding immediate expensing (first-year Capital Cost Allowance) to over 65% of business assets, including patents and software alongside pipelines, vehicles, and roads. Tax auditors and corporate planners must distinguish these instruments: the Productivity Mega Deduction is a cost-based accelerated depreciation (CCA) measure on asset acquisitions, not an income-based Patent Box preference limited to IP-derived income. As of November 2026, Canada has not enacted a federal Patent Box regime.
Section 2: Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Framework
2.1 Analysis of Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

For all federal income tax purposes, subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory definition is structured into three operational tiers: primary research and development categories (paragraphs (a) to (c)), eligible support work (paragraph (d)), and explicitly excluded activities (paragraphs (e) to (k)).
Primary SR&ED Categories (Paragraphs 248(1)(a) to (c))

The first tier establishes the three foundational categories of scientific or technological work. Under paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research is work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph 248(1)(b), applied research is work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph 248(1)(c), experimental development is work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development is the most commonly claimed category of SR&ED in Canada and expressly encompasses incremental improvements, provided the work seeks to generate or discover technological knowledge or know-how that advances the taxpayer's technological knowledge base rather than applying routine engineering.
Eligible Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d))

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), SR&ED includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight enumerated disciplines: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research (defined in the CRA SR&ED Glossary as an approach involving mathematical treatment of a process, problem, or operation to determine its purpose, effectiveness, and maximum efficiency), (4) mathematical analysis (the examination of a set of observations using mathematical tools, principles, methods, or techniques), (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, and (8) psychological research. Crucially, work in these eight areas is never eligible on its own (unless an engineer or computer scientist is directly performing basic research, applied research, or experimental development under paragraphs (a) to (c)). To qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d), the support work must satisfy a dual statutory nexus: it must be commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
Statutorily Excluded Work (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))
Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes from SR&ED any work with respect to seven specified categories:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion (work that supplements advertising and personal selling, coordinating them and making them effective).

Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes (techniques and work that sustain the quality of a product or service to satisfy given requirements).
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities.
Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas.
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes.
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As clarified in the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, excluded work is considered only after eligible SR&ED work has been identified. Conducting an excluded activity (such as prospecting for minerals or commercial production) does not disqualify other eligible SR&ED work performed at the same time, provided the excluded portion is separated from the claim. Moreover, the distinguishing factor between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as data collection or testing) and excluded work under paragraphs (f) or (k) (routine testing or routine data collection) is the purpose of the work: if data collection is carried out as part of normal business operations or quality control, it is excluded; if it is carried out specifically to directly support SR&ED experimentation or analysis, it is eligible as support work.
2.2 CRA Eligibility Methodology: The "Why" and "How" Framework vs. The Five Questions

On August 13, 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), the CRA published the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, formally replacing and archiving its prior Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (dated April 24, 2015).

Under the archived 2015 policy, the CRA evaluated work under a two-step methodology ("Step 1: Determine if there is SR&ED" and "Step 2: Determine the extent of eligible work") anchored by Five Questions derived from the Tax Court of Canada's landmark decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen:

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: The current CRA Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives consolidate these principles into two mandatory requirements that must both be satisfied—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement—while the Federal Court of Appeal has confirmed (in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72) that the underlying five-part legal test from Northwest Hydraulic remains the binding judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1).
The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty)

Work satisfies the "Why" requirement when it is conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement. The key objective is generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories or prediction models) that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely gathering factual knowledge (such as basic data or measurements). Categorizing the knowledge as specifically scientific versus technological is not required, as both are eligible.

New scientific or technological knowledge is needed when it is unknown or uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved—or how to achieve it—due to an insufficiency in the available scientific or technological knowledge. Available knowledge includes the combined scientific and technological knowledge within the business together with publicly available sources reasonably accessible to the business. The recognition of scientific or technological uncertainty marks the starting point for SR&ED work, while scientific or technological advancement is the targeted outcome.

In experimental development, characteristics suggesting an insufficiency of technological knowledge include situations where existing design methods are not applicable, requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards, too many variables or unknowns are present, parameters or conditions fall outside the normal operating range, the nature of the problem is evolving, data is not readily available, or interlocking constraints exist. While cost targets alone do not create technological uncertainty, attempting to meet cost targets under technical constraints may create a technological uncertainty imposed by economic considerations. Experimental development commonly occurs when generating entirely new technology to meet an objective, making improvements to existing technology, or applying existing technology in a new environment or context (such as scaling up and optimizing processes for rapid vaccine production).

If technological uncertainty is ignored or circumvented with a workaround using available knowledge, the work is not eligible; work is eligible only when an attempt is made to resolve the uncertainty to generate or discover new scientific or technological knowledge. Finally, success or failure in meeting project objectives is irrelevant when assessing whether work meets the "Why" requirement—only the underlying purpose of attempting to achieve advancement is evaluated.
The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

Work satisfies the "How" requirement when it is a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Simply following a systematic approach or standard business procedures is insufficient. The required systematic investigation comprises four core steps:

items: Generating an Idea or Hypothesis: Formulating an idea consistent with known facts (expressed as a possible solution to a problem, a proposed method, or an approach) that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving an objective or resolving a problem.
Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, recognizing that the idea can evolve and change as a result of testing.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Formulating logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis.
Keeping Evidence: Retaining documentation and evidence that is generated as the work progresses.

body.text: 2.3 Special Operational Contexts: Assets, Prototypes, Pilot Plants, and Production Runs

When SR&ED is performed in industrial, manufacturing, or commercial environments, two specialized CRA policies govern the boundary between eligible experimental development and excluded commercial production: the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (updated July 6, 2023) and the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (updated July 19, 2016).
SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy

In the context of SR&ED, an asset is a material, device, product, or process facility, classified into four categories: (1) pilot plant, (2) commercial plant, (3) prototype, and (4) custom product or commercial asset. SR&ED eligibility must be established before determining the type of asset resulting from the SR&ED so that project costs can be apportioned accurately between SR&ED and commercial activities.

A pilot plant is a non-commercial-scale production facility developed primarily for carrying out SR&ED during its useful life, isolated from normal business operations and sized specifically for the SR&ED to be conducted. It is used solely for technical or experimental content to systematically investigate processing steps under conditions simulating a full production unit—obtaining data to evaluate hypotheses, establishing finished product technical specifications and process/product formulae, designing special equipment and structures for new or improved fabrication processes, studying raw material behaviour, and testing unproven equipment or processes.

With respect to prototypes and duplicate copies of a prototype, constructing duplicate copies of a prototype after successful testing to satisfy inventory or customer demand is not SR&ED. However, expenditures (labour, materials, and overhead) to construct duplicate copies of a prototype for testing may qualify as materials for SR&ED (consumed or transformed) when the tests are completed—rather than when the copies are initially constructed—provided the testing directly supports basic research, applied research, or experimental development prior to commercial production/use and is commensurate with the research needs. For example, if a supplier develops a prototype part, builds 100 duplicate copies for testing on a manufacturer's line where they are damaged during testing, and receives $100,000 from the manufacturer, the copies qualify as materials transformed in SR&ED (rather than a commercial custom product), though ITC recapture rules apply upon disposition.

For custom products and commercial assets, if components requiring SR&ED work do not significantly affect non-SR&ED components, work on the unaffected components is ineligible; conversely, if SR&ED on a component requires redesigning closely associated components, the redesign of those associated components may qualify. Only materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED work can be claimed, and ITC recapture rules apply when the custom product or commercial asset is sold or converted to commercial use. Where apportioning costs between SR&ED and commercial work on a custom product or commercial asset is extremely difficult, the CRA permits an Alternative Approach for Cost Allocation under either the traditional method or the proxy method, calculated as:

Allowable SR&ED expenditures = (A − B) + C, where A is the total actual costs of developing the custom product or commercial asset; B is the estimated costs that would usually be associated with building the asset if the technology had already existed; and C is an estimated amount for the cost of materials transformed in SR&ED.
SR&ED During Production Runs Policy

When experimental development (ED) is carried out during the operation of equipment or processes within a manufacturing environment, the CRA categorizes the production run context into one of two classifications based on technical risk (such as process modifications risking product specification changes or process instability, uncertain efficiency of a new process combination, yield losses exceeding normal levels, or equipment damage) and contemporaneously documented experimental protocols (specific experimental operating instructions, senior management authorization of technical risk, direct supervision by qualified technical personnel, and production quantities restricted strictly to experimental project needs):

items: ED+EP (Experimental Development Resulting in Experimental Production): Experimental production (EP) is output needed to verify whether SR&ED objectives have been met or if a technological advancement is achievable (including pilot plant operation). Under ED+EP, salaries and wages are allowable for employees directly engaged in ED work resulting in required EP (including non-specialized shop-floor employees needed to produce EP), and materials consumed or transformed into required EP output are fully allowable (subject to ITC recapture on transformed materials if sold). Any production beyond what is required to evaluate or validate the SR&ED project is deemed excess production, and all labour, overhead, and material costs for excess production are strictly disallowed.

ED+CP (Experimental Development Conducted in Conjunction or Simultaneously with Commercial Production): Where ED occurs simultaneously with commercial production (CP), costs attributable to normal commercial production and input costs incurred before the start of the SR&ED portion of the run are disallowed. Only the incremental costs of salaries/wages, materials consumed or transformed, and (under the traditional method) overhead directly attributable to the ED work—calculated by subtracting standard commercial production costs from actual trial production costs—are allowable.

body.text: Section 3: Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Refundability, and Pool Mechanics
3.1 The Subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year may accumulate allowable expenditures for SR&ED carried on in Canada in a cumulative deductible pool.

The pool aggregates current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a)—comprising salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, SR&ED contracts performed on behalf of the claimant (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), third-party payments (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii)), and, under the traditional method, directly attributable overhead and post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs (or eligible ≥90% / >50% equipment lease costs under the proxy method)—together with post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b), repayments of government or non-government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(c), and prior-year ITC recapture additions. Under subsection 37(4), no amount may be deducted in respect of an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED. Furthermore, when an expenditure could be deductible as either an SR&ED expenditure or a charitable donation, the amount must be deducted as an SR&ED expenditure and not as a charitable donation.

The subsection 37(1) pool is reduced by government assistance and non-government assistance (paragraph 37(1)(d)) and provincial super-allowance benefit amounts (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)) that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing-due date, as well as by federal SR&ED ITCs applied or refunded in the preceding taxation year and proceeds of disposition of SR&ED capital property (reported at Line 440 of Form T661). If the reductions to the pool exceed the positive balance of the pool otherwise calculated, the excess amount must be included in the taxpayer's net income for the taxation year. Notably, contract payments received by an SR&ED performer reduce the performer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9), but do not reduce the performer's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.

Deductions from the subsection 37(1) pool are optional in any given taxation year. Any positive undeducted balance is tracked by the CRA as a running balance that never expires and may be carried forward indefinitely to be deducted against business income in any subsequent taxation year. Using an amount from the subsection 37(1) pool in a subsequent taxation year is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline, provided the SR&ED expenditures comprising the pool were identified on time on Form T661 in the year incurred. Moreover, when a corporate claimant performs SR&ED related to a business actively engaged in by a related corporation (such as a wholly owned subsidiary performing research for its parent corporation, determined without reference to control by right), the SR&ED is considered to be related to a business of the claimant.
Special pool rules govern partnerships and corporate control changes:

items: Partnerships: Under the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy and Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, a partnership cannot carry forward an amount in the subsection 37(1) pool to a subsequent fiscal period; the pool balance at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be fully deducted in calculating the partnership's net income for tax purposes in that year. Furthermore, SR&ED ITCs allocated to partners reduce the partnership's subsection 37(1) pool in the same fiscal period (unlike corporations and individuals, where applied or refunded ITCs reduce the pool in the subsequent year), while any partnership SR&ED ITC recapture excess added to partners' Part I tax increases the partnership pool in the subsequent year. Crucially, a partnership loss created or increased by deducting the subsection 37(1) pool is not allowed to a limited partner (the limited partner's deductible loss is reduced by the lesser of the SR&ED pool deduction and the partnership loss, and the disallowed loss cannot be claimed by other partners, does not become a limited partnership loss or non-capital loss, and does not adjust the limited partner's adjusted cost base).

Loss Restriction Events (Subsection 37(6.1)): When an acquisition of control occurs for a corporation (or a trust acquires a new majority-interest beneficiary), a deemed taxation year-end occurs immediately prior to the event, and the undeducted subsection 37(1) pool is reduced to nil unless two streaming conditions are satisfied in the subsequent taxation year: (1) the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related is continued for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and (2) the deduction is claimed only to the extent of income for the taxation year (before making any subsection 37(1) deduction) derived from that same business or a similar business.

body.text: 3.2 Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates and Expenditure Limit Calculations

Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), claimants earn an ITC calculated as a percentage of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year.

The basic ITC rate is 15% and applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures of corporations (other than CCPCs and ECPCs within their annual expenditure limit), sole proprietorships (individuals), beneficiaries of trusts, and partners of a partnership, as well as to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their expenditure limit for the taxation year.

The enhanced ITC rate is 35% (comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement under paragraph 127(9)(a.1) and subsection 127(10.1) over the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool minus provincial super-allowance benefit amounts). For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, only CCPCs qualified for the 35% enhanced rate up to a maximum $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (pursuant to Bill C-15), both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn the 35% enhanced rate up to a doubled maximum annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000.

Under subsection 127(9), an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) is a Canadian public corporation that is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by non-resident persons; even if all shares of the corporation owned by non-residents were hypothetically owned by one particular person, an ECPC would still not be controlled by that particular person.
Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Rules and Group Allocations

Where a CCPC is associated with other corporations (subsection 127(10.3)) or an ECPC is a member of a consolidated group (subsection 127(10.61)), the group must share a single annual expenditure limit allocated via a prescribed agreement form (Schedule T2SCH49 for CCPCs; a separate prescribed form is published for consolidated ECPCs and revenue-electing CCPCs). Under subsections 127(10.4) and 127(10.63), if the corporate group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days of a request by the CRA, the Minister may allocate the expenditure limit among the members of the group. If a corporation has a short taxation year (fewer than 51 weeks), its expenditure limit is prorated based on the number of days in the taxation year; if a corporation has multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the expenditure limit for each taxation year equals the limit for the first taxation year (subject to proration for short years).
The annual expenditure limit is reduced according to corporation type and taxation year:

items: For a CCPC Whose Taxation Year Begins Before December 16, 2024: The $3,000,000 maximum expenditure limit begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and its associated corporations) for the previous taxation year reaches $10,000,000, and becomes nil starting at $50,000,000.

For a CCPC Whose Taxation Year Begins After December 15, 2024 (Subsection 127(10.2)): Under the default taxable capital method, the $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada for the previous taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil starting at $75,000,000. Alternatively, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a CCPC (or all associated CCPCs in an associated group acting jointly) may elect on the prescribed form to calculate its expenditure limit using the 3-year average annual revenue method applicable to ECPCs.

For an ECPC (and Electing CCPC) Whose Taxation Year Begins After December 15, 2024 (Subsections 127(10.6) and 127(10.61)): Under the revenue method, the $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit is reduced based on the total of all amounts of average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for each corporation in the consolidated or associated group over the preceding 3 fiscal years (or the actual number of fiscal years if fewer than 3), regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire 3-year period. The expenditure limit begins to decrease when average annual revenue exceeds $15,000,000, and becomes nil starting at $75,000,000.

body.text: 3.3 Refundability Rules, Qualifying Corporations, and Carryover Mechanics

A claimant must first apply its earned SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(5) to reduce to nil its Part I federal income tax otherwise payable in the current taxation year. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash to the claimant in the taxation year is deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in the year, thereby reducing the ITCs available for carryback or carryforward.
Under section 127.1 and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, refundability depends on the entity's classification:

items: Qualifying Corporation (Subsection 127.1(2)): A CCPC throughout the taxation year whose taxable income for the previous taxation year (or the total taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit.

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024: $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) / $40,000,000], where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount is ≤ $10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which the taxable capital amount exceeds $10,000,000.

body.text: Carryback, Carryforward, Trust/Partnership Allocations, and Acquisition of Control

Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back up to 3 prior taxation years or carried forward for up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable, expiring if unapplied after 20 years. Where a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (Section 5.1 of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy), unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control are restricted from being carried forward freely, and unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control are restricted from being carried back to taxation years prior to the acquisition of control.

For trusts, a beneficiary's reasonably designated portion of an SR&ED ITC is added to the beneficiary's ITC for the taxation year; however, only graduated rate estates and communal organizations deemed inter vivos trusts can designate an ITC to their beneficiaries. For partnerships (subsection 127(8) and the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy), the ITC is always calculated at the 15% basic rate at the partnership level (even if a partner is a CCPC) and allocated to partners in proportion to their agreed share of partnership income or loss. However, no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of a partnership (such as a limited partner or a passive general partner). Any unallocated ITC belonging to specified members is reallocated to the active (non-specified) general partners based on what is reasonable having regard to their investment (including debt obligations) in the partnership. An active partner receiving reallocated ITCs from a specified member may elect to renounce any portion of those reallocated credits using Form T932 (Election by a Member of a Partnership to Renounce Investment Tax Credits Pursuant to Subsection 127(8.4)), which extinguishes the renounced ITC without reducing the partnership's subsection 37(1) expenditure pool.
Section 4: Qualified Expenditures, Overhead Calculation Methods, and Capital Restoration
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B))

Under subsection 37(8) and subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, a claimant must select one of two mutually exclusive methods for calculating SR&ED expenditures for each taxation year: the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) or the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)). To use the Proxy Method, the claimant must explicitly elect it on Form T661 when the first claim for the taxation year is filed; if no election is made, the Traditional Method applies automatically. The choice of method is irrevocable for the taxation year once Form T661 is filed and cannot be changed subsequently.
