body.text: Mechanics of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4)–(10)

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated March 27, 2026), the PPA is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 as 55% of the salary base, subject to an overall PPA cap. Because the PPA is a notional amount, it is included in "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) solely to earn SR&ED ITCs; claimants do not include the PPA in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, while the actual overhead and other expenditures represented by the PPA remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1).

In computing the salary base for any employee (whether a specified employee or not), Regulation 2900(9) strictly excludes four items: (1) taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 of the Act; (2) unpaid amounts from a prior year paid in the current taxation year that are deemed to be expenditures incurred in the year (Line 310 of Form T661); (3) remuneration based on profits; and (4) bonuses.

Furthermore, Regulation 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA to ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed total business expenditures made in the taxation year:

PPA ≤ A − B − C, where A is the total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of specific deductions claimed in the year under sections 20 (e.g., CCA, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing to carry on business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED expenditures), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development), and 104 (trusts) of the Act; and C is expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (other than a prescribed special-purpose building). If a claimant carries on more than one business, specified amounts deducted across all businesses must be aggregated; in general, the overall cap does not restrict the PPA if the claimant deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED expenses for each $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.
Worked Numerical Comparison: Traditional vs. Proxy Method (Acme Ltd.)

In Section 6.0 of the Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, the CRA illustrates the calculation for Acme Ltd., a CCPC entitled to the 35% enhanced ITC rate that incurs $100,000 in SR&ED employee salaries, $15,000 in SR&ED materials, and $50,000 in SR&ED overhead expenditures:

items: Under the Traditional Method: Additions to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool total $165,000 ($100,000 salaries + $15,000 materials + $50,000 overhead); the PPA is $0; total qualified SR&ED expenditures equal $165,000; and the total ITC earned at 35% is $57,750.

Under the Proxy Method: Additions to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool total $115,000 ($100,000 salaries + $15,000 materials, with the $50,000 overhead deducted separately as an ordinary business expense); the PPA (55% of the $100,000 salary base) equals $55,000; total qualified SR&ED expenditures equal $170,000 ($115,000 + $55,000); and the total ITC earned at 35% is $59,500.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, Foreign Work, and the 180-Day Rule

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (generally relating to gross wages reported on an employee's T4 slip for the calendar year). Salaries or drawings paid or payable to sole proprietors or partners are not employment income (T4) and are not deductible or qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Under the Proxy Method, only salaries or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (determined by hands-on tasks performed rather than job title, including non-specialized employees performing direct SR&ED work) may be claimed. Under the Traditional Method, salaries or wages for employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED are claimed, and administrative salaries or wages for clerical and administrative staff providing support directly to SR&ED employees may be claimed on Line 360 as SR&ED overhead if they are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED. Where an employee spends all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) of their time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, Regulation 2900(5) and clause 37(8)(a)(ii) deem 100% of their eligible salary or wages to be for SR&ED.

Cash outlays for taxable benefits (section 6 of the Act, such as automobile benefits, housing, board, meals, gifts, awards, low-interest loans, group term life insurance, and tuition fees) are allowable. Non-cash taxable benefits may only be included in SR&ED salary or wages if (1) the value claimed is a reasonable estimate of the actual costs incurred by the employer, (2) the value excludes any GST/HST or PST (unless no input tax credit/refund can be claimed), and (3) the actual underlying costs (including CCA) are not claimed as a business expense under section 9. Conversely, four categories are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages: (1) the employer's share of related benefits (CPP, QPP, EI, WSIB, CNESST, approved employee pension plans, and medical/dental/optical insurance plans—which are only claimable as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method), (2) extended vacation or sick leave, (3) stock option benefits (section 7 and subsections 143.3(3) and 143.3(5)), and (4) retiring allowances.
Strict Restrictions on "Specified Employees"

A specified employee (an employee who is a specified shareholder owning ≥10% of the shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer) is subject to three cumulative statutory limits:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9) ITA): An expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada does not include any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid or accrued to a specified employee under either the Traditional or Proxy Method. (For employees other than specified employees, bonuses and profit-based remuneration are allowable in the subsection 37(1) pool—and if an employee's only remuneration for SR&ED work in the year consists of bonuses or profit-based remuneration, a portion commensurate with those duties is accepted—though they remain excluded from the Proxy salary base under Regulation 2900(9).)

Subsection 37(1) Pool Cap – 5 × YMPE (Section 6.0, SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy): The maximum SR&ED salary or wages of a specified employee that can be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure in the subsection 37(1) pool is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) (determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends), prorated for the number of days the individual is a specified employee during the taxation year. Where a specified employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations (including related individuals or partnerships deemed associated), the total aggregated SR&ED salary claimed across all associated corporations cannot exceed 5 × YMPE, and each associated corporation must file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) together with a certified copy of the Directors' resolution authorizing the agreement (or a signed confirmation from a sole shareholder who owns both corporations) no later than its respective SR&ED reporting deadline; if Form T1174 is not filed by the reporting deadline, the specified employee's salary or wages are deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure.

Proxy Salary Base Cap – Lesser of 75% of Salary or 2.5 × YMPE (Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8)): When computing the salary base for the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method, the amount included for a specified employee cannot exceed the lesser of:
75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); OR

2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days of employment in the taxation year (2.5 × A × B / 365), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for time the employee was not a specified employee), shared across all associated corporations employing that individual in taxation years ending in the same calendar year (Regulation 2900(8) and 2900(10)).

body.text: Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Work Performed Outside Canada (Section 10.0)

Except for permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada, foreign R&D expenditures cannot be included in the subsection 37(1) pool or earn ITCs (though current expenditures for foreign R&D may be deducted in computing net business income under subsection 37(2)). Under Section 10.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada by employees may be included in allowable SR&ED salaries and wages if (1) the work is performed solely in support of SR&ED carried on within Canada by the claimant, (2) the salary or wages paid are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country, and (3) the claim complies with the 10% limit on Form T661.
The 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rules (Subsection 78(4) vs. Subsection 127(26))
The Income Tax Act enforces two distinct 180-day payment rules depending on whether the unpaid expenditure is employee remuneration versus another current SR&ED expense:

items: Unpaid Salary or Wages (Subsection 78(4) ITA): Employee remuneration that is not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year for both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) ITC calculation. When paid in a subsequent year, it is deemed incurred in the year paid (identified on Line 310 of Form T661, where it remains excluded from the Proxy salary base under Regulation 2900(9)).

Unpaid Current Expenditures Other Than Salary or Wages (Subsection 127(26) ITA): Any current SR&ED expenditure other than salary, wages, or other remuneration (such as materials or subcontractor invoices) that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year is still included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the year incurred, but strictly for ITC purposes is deemed not to have been incurred in that year and instead to be incurred at the time it is actually paid. The claimant must identify the unpaid current expenditure on Form T661 by the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for the year incurred, and then claim the expenditure for ITC purposes on the "payment of prior years' unpaid amounts (other than salary or wages)" line of Form T661 in the subsequent year when paid (entering 80% of the amount paid if it was an arm's length SR&ED contract expenditure).

body.text: 4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, the cost of materials of a current nature purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers is claimable under both the Traditional Method (Regulation 2900(2)(a)) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)) if the materials are consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (and paid within the taxation year or within 180 days of year-end for ITC purposes). To qualify as materials for SR&ED rather than overhead, the items must, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a thing upon which the SR&ED is being performed. Broken or used lab supplies, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants (such as engine oil) do not compose the body of the thing being worked on and can only be claimed as overhead under the Traditional Method.

items: Materials Consumed: "Consumed" means absorbed, used up, destroyed, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of SR&ED. Under the 90% rule, if 90% or more of the cost of a material is consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED, the entire cost of that material is allowable.

Animals, Growing Things, Energy, and Water: Animal feed, plant fertilizer, pesticides, herbicides, and fungicides used for animals or growing things in SR&ED qualify as materials consumed (restricted to incremental cost if conducted alongside commercial production). While general utilities (electricity, fuel, oil, natural gas, utility washdown water, and boiler feed water) are overhead claimable only under the Traditional Method, energy qualifies as a material for SR&ED under both methods in endothermic reactions requiring significant direct energy input where intermediate or final products retain that energy (such as chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, metallurgical refining, cement, glass, ceramics, and plastics forming), and process water that enters the process, becomes part of an intermediate or final product, and is rendered valueless as process feed qualifies as a material consumed.

Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)): Materials transformed are materials changed or incorporated into another material or product as a result of SR&ED that still retain some value to the claimant or a third party (such as a commercial sale value greater than 10% of original costs). Under the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 14, 2022), if property incorporating transformed materials (or SR&ED contract property or SUE/capital property) on which an SR&ED ITC was earned in any of the 20 preceding taxation years is sold or converted to commercial use, subsection 127(27) triggers ITC Recapture. The recaptured amount—calculated at the rate (15% or 35%) at which the original ITC was earned on the lesser of the original cost of the property and the proceeds of disposition (arm's length sale) or fair market value (conversion to commercial use or non-arm's length disposition)—is reported on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND), added directly to Part I tax payable for the year, and increases the claimant's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures for the subsequent taxation year. Crucially, under subsections 127(27) and 127(32), if a claimant orders a part from an arm's length supplier for $12,000, the full $12,000 is subject to recapture; however, if the claimant manufactures the part in-house or pulls an item from its own manufactured inventory (e.g., a batch of boxes costing $12 comprising $3 labour, $7 arm's length material, and $2 overhead), only the cost of the materials originally purchased ($7) is subject to recapture—there is no recapture on in-house manufacturing or SR&ED salaries and overhead.

body.text: 4.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transfers (Form T1146), and Third-Party Payments (Form T1263)
Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts and the 80% Inclusion Rate

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, when a claimant contracts an arm's length party to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada, 100% of the current contract expenditure is included in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool, and 80% of the contract expenditure qualifies for ITC calculation purposes under paragraph 127(9)(g). Where a contract combines SR&ED and non-SR&ED work, the total contract price must be allocated reasonably (e.g., based on fair market value), and the 80% inclusion rate applies strictly to the SR&ED portion. If a claimant contracts out only paragraph 248(1)(d) support work to an arm's length contractor, the payer may claim the expenditure if the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the payer's Canadian SR&ED, whereas the contractor cannot claim SR&ED on standalone support work.

Under the Taxable Supplier Rules (Subsection 127(9)), an arm's length contract expenditure qualifies for ITCs only if it is paid or payable to, or for the benefit of, a taxable supplier—meaning a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident person/partnership that carries on business through a permanent establishment in Canada. For example, if Canadian corporation H Limited contracts out SR&ED for $1,000 to foreign corporation F Limited (which has no permanent establishment in Canada and is not a taxable supplier), and F Limited subcontracts the work to Canadian corporation J Limited for $900 (which incurs $850 in SR&ED costs), H Limited can include the $1,000 in its subsection 37(1) deductible pool but gets $0 in qualified expenditures for ITCs, while J Limited claims the $850 for both its subsection 37(1) pool and its ITCs without reducing its qualified expenditures by the $900 payment received from non-taxable supplier F Limited.

Furthermore, while between 2014 and December 15, 2024, the look-through rule under former subsection 37(14) required a payer to reduce its SR&ED contract expenditure by any non-current (capital) expenditures incurred by the contractor (with written notice required from the performer within 90 days of calendar year-end under subsection 37(15)), the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026) confirms that contract expenditures and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024, will generally no longer be reduced by capital expenditures of the SR&ED performer.
Non-Arm's Length (NAL) Contracts and Transfers of Qualified Expenditures (Form T1146)

Under subsection 127(24), expenditures (other than employee salary or wages) incurred for SR&ED performed by a person or partnership with whom the claimant does not deal at arm's length (NAL) are excluded (0% eligible) from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. However, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer (transferor) and NAL payer (transferee) may file a joint agreement on Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures (including the performer's 55% PPA, and post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures) to the payer, with the performer deducting the transferred amount on Line 540 of Form T661.
Under Section 4.0 of the Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, strict 180-day payment rules govern NAL transfers on Form T1146:

items: The contract payment from the NAL payer to the NAL performer must be paid on or before the day that is 180 days after the end of the performer's taxation year; if the payer pays only $5,000 of a $10,000 contract within 180 days, the maximum transferable amount is permanently capped at $5,000.

The underlying qualified expenditures incurred by the NAL performer must also be paid by the performer on or before the day that is 180 days after the end of the performer's taxation year; if a performer incurs $9,000 of qualified expenditures in Year 1 but pays only $3,000 within 180 days (paying the remaining $6,000 in Year 2), only $3,000 can be transferred to the payer for Year 1, and the remaining $6,000 cannot be transferred for Year 1 or Year 2.

body.text: When an SR&ED performer purchases goods (materials) or non-SR&ED services from a NAL supplier (subsections 127(11.5) and 127(11.6)), no inter-company profit may be included in qualified expenditures; the cost to the performer is restricted to the adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost incurred by the NAL party that acquired the property or rendered the service at arm's length.
Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) & Form T1263)

Under the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, a claimant may deduct 100% in its subsection 37(1) pool and include 80% in its qualified expenditures for ITC purposes for payments made to six categories of external entities (Entities A through F) to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada, provided the SR&ED is related to a business of the claimant, the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED, and the claimant files Form T1263 (Third-party payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)):

items: Entity A (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)): Corporations resident in Canada.
Entity B (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): Approved associations.

Entity C (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): Approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or similar institutions (Canadian universities and affiliated colleges are automatically considered "approved"; other entities must apply for formal Ministerial approval through the CRA Income Tax Rulings Directorate).
Entity D (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): Non-profit SR&ED corporations resident in Canada exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j).
Entity E (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): Approved granting councils or organizations that forward payments to Entity B, C, or D.

Entity F (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)): Available only to corporate claimants, for payments to a tax-exempt paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada specifically for basic or applied research carried on in Canada.

body.text: Third-party payments differ fundamentally from contract expenditures: in a third-party payment, control of the SR&ED is held by the performer rather than the payer, rights to the research are non-exclusive (results are generally published, though the payer receives preferential rights to exploit the results), there is usually more than one funder, the research is typically basic or applied research, and tax incentives are earned on a cash basis in the year paid (except for Entity A), whereas contract expenditures are earned on an accrual basis in the year the work is performed. Payments in kind to an approved university or college are valued at the fair market value of the property or service provided, provided there are no conditions involving direct or indirect payments back to the claimant. Special third-party payment provisions also allow agricultural producers to earn ITCs on agricultural check-off dues paid to agricultural organizations that fund SR&ED as agents for the producers, as well as payments supporting university research chairs.
4.5 Overhead, Cloud Computing, and Software Costs (Regulations 2900(2)(c), 2900(3), and 2902)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022), SR&ED overhead and other expenditures can only be claimed under the Traditional Method (reported on Line 360 of Form T661). To qualify under paragraph 2900(2)(c) or subsection 2900(3) of the Regulations, the claimant must link the expenditure to SR&ED using a rational and reasonable method that satisfies two cumulative tests:

items: Directly Related to the Prosecution of SR&ED: The expenditure must connect directly to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by SR&ED staff, with no intervening step or intermediary. For hands-on SR&ED employees, related benefits, retiring allowances, training costs in Canada, and travel expenses (including travel for testing at a customer location in Canada or training travel) may be directly linked to SR&ED work; by contrast, for clerical and administrative staff, while incremental salaries and wages directly linked to SR&ED are allowable on Line 360, their related benefits, retiring allowances, training, and travel have only an indirect link to SR&ED and are not allowed.

Incremental: The expenditure (or portion thereof) would not have been incurred if the prosecution of SR&ED (or the provision of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment) had not occurred. Consequently, fixed-cost maintenance contracts generally fail the incremental test, and waste disposal costs are not considered directly related and incremental once the SR&ED activity that produced the scrap has finished. Other qualifying incremental overheads include telephone/cellular/internet costs, utilities, periodical subscriptions, volunteer fees and related costs for clinical studies, selection and hiring expenses for SR&ED personnel, and health and safety expenses.

body.text: With respect to cloud computing and software, cloud infrastructure used specifically for experimental prototypes or R&D testing is eligible (as incremental overhead under the Traditional Method or implicitly covered via the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method), whereas production cloud infrastructure is ineligible. Under Section 6 of the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), for software and software licensing expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024: software intended to be directly incorporated into a commercial product cannot be included in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, whereas software purchased solely as a tool to execute SR&ED (such as computer-aided design software) may qualify—either as a current expense if the acquisition benefits only the current fiscal period, or as a capital expenditure (depreciable property) if the software provides an enduring benefit beyond one year (useful life > 1 year).

Finally, under section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations (and Section 4.8 of the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy), specific prescribed expenditures are strictly non-qualifying even if directly related and incremental to SR&ED: (1) SR&ED claim preparation fees, (2) convention or conference attendance costs, (3) interest expenses, (4) charitable donations (Regulation 2902(d)), and (5) acquisition of rights in or arising out of SR&ED (Regulation 2902(c)).
4.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) and the publication of the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), expenditures for depreciable property and equipment leases acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024, qualify for SR&ED tax incentives (whereas capital and lease expenditures before December 16, 2024, remain ineligible).
Full SR&ED Capital Expenditures (90% ASA Test – Paragraph 37(1)(b))

To qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure (claimed on Line 390 of Form T661, with the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties per project entered on Lines 262 and 263), the expenditure must be made to acquire new or used depreciable property (other than a building, a leasehold interest in a building, non-depreciable land, inventory, or goodwill) acquired after December 15, 2024, that at the time of acquisition was intended by the claimant to be used in one of two ways (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III)):

items: Used during All or Substantially All (ASA, 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED carried on in Canada; OR

Have All or Substantially All (ASA, 90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada (e.g., due to rapid technological obsolescence or destruction during testing, in which case the overall length of the SR&ED project is irrelevant).

body.text: Intent at the time of acquisition is evaluated based on the reason for purchase, potential and actual use, project length, past practices on similar property, and project planning documents or business cases. Capital cost includes the purchase price, legal, accounting, engineering, and installation fees, customs and excise duties, transportation, significant storage costs, and additions or improvements (for self-manufactured property, it includes material, labour, and overhead costs, excluding any profit element).

Qualifying SR&ED capital expenditures are included in the subsection 37(1)(b) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Any amount deducted from the pool for an SR&ED capital expenditure is deemed to be an amount allowed as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) in a separate prescribed class, preventing duplicate CCA claims on Schedule T2SCH8 (if a capital expenditure is not claimed on Form T661 by the SR&ED reporting deadline, it must be classified on Schedule T2SCH8 under standard CCA rules). When SR&ED capital property is sold or disposed of, the lesser of the proceeds of disposition and the undeducted balance of expenditures for that property is reported at Line 440 of Form T661 to reduce the undeducted pool balance; if proceeds exceed the undeducted expenditure balance, the excess is included in income on Schedule T2SCH1 as recaptured CCA up to the original cost.

For Investment Tax Credit (ITC) purposes, inclusion in the subsection 37(1)(b) pool does not automatically guarantee ITC qualification: under paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations, the acquisition or refurbishment of used property is a prescribed expenditure that does not qualify for SR&ED ITCs—only new depreciable property earns ITCs (and purchases from non-arm's length parties have their qualified expenditure amount restricted). Up to the corporation's expenditure limit ($6,000,000), the 35% enhanced ITC earned on capital expenditures is 40% refundable.
Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Primary Use >50% to <90% – Subsection 127(9))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that is used for both SR&ED and commercial work and does not meet the 90% ASA criteria is not part of the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (it must be depreciated under regular CCA rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH8). However, under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods, it may earn SR&ED ITCs on Line 504 of Form T661 (with the 20 most expensive SUE items named on the form) as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE):

items: First Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): 25% of the capital cost of the equipment qualifies for ITCs if the property: (1) is depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024; (2) does not meet the 90% ASA criterion; (3) is not a Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11); (4) is not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF); (5) is new property (not previously used, acquired to be used, or rented for any purpose prior to acquisition); and (6) is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the first period (beginning when the property is acquired and available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that occurs at least 12 months after acquisition).

Second Term SUE (Additional 25% of Capital Cost, Totaling 50%): An additional 25% of the capital cost qualifies for ITCs if the property qualified as First Term SUE and is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the second period (beginning when acquired and available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that is at least 24 months after acquisition/availability).

Exclusion of Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP – Regulation 2900(11)): A property is disqualified as a PDP (earning 0% SUE ITCs) if it meets both parts of the two-part PDP intent test at the time of acquisition: (1) Commercial Integration Intent—the claimant intended at acquisition to use the property for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a facility, plant, or line for commercial manufacturing, commercial processing, or another commercial purpose; AND (2) Primary Non-SR&ED Lifetime Use Intent—the claimant intended at acquisition to use the property during its operating time over its expected useful life primarily for purposes other than SR&ED (or consume its value primarily in non-SR&ED activities). If a claimant can support that at acquisition it intended to use the equipment primarily for SR&ED over its expected useful life, and only converted it due to unforeseen circumstances, the property is not a PDP.

SUE ITC Recapture Example: If SUE is sold or all or substantially all of it is converted to commercial use within 20 years, ITC recapture applies to the lesser of the SUE ITC obtained and the ITC rate applied to 25% (if First Term only) or 50% (if First and Second Term) of the proceeds of disposition or fair market value. As illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, if equipment is acquired on February 13, 2025, for $160,000 by a CCPC (35% ITC rate), earning $14,000 First Term SUE ITC (35% × 25% × $160,000) and $14,000 Second Term SUE ITC (totaling $28,000 ITC), and is sold in 2028 for $100,000, the recapture amount is the lesser of $28,000 and $17,500 (35% × $100,000 × 50%), resulting in $17,500 of recaptured ITC.

body.text: Equipment and Building Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease expenditures for equipment incurred after December 15, 2024, qualify as follows (if a taxation year straddles December 15, 2024, SR&ED use is calculated as a percentage of total operating time for the period after December 15, 2024):

items: Traditional Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II), Regulation 2900(2)(c)): When leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease expenditure is claimable as a lease cost. When leased equipment is used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED after December 15, 2024, the lease cost is claimable on Line 360 of Form T661 as overhead and other expenditures in proportion to the percentage the leased equipment is used for SR&ED, provided it is directly attributable (directly related and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under the Traditional Method, the cost of leasing land incurred after December 15, 2024, may also be claimed on Line 360 if it is ASA attributable or directly attributable to SR&ED in Canada.

Proxy Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI)): After December 15, 2024, if leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimable. If leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used more than 50% but less than 90% (primarily) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost is claimable. If leased equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% can be claimed under the Proxy Method. Furthermore, under the Proxy Method, lease costs for General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) and land are strictly excluded.

Building Lease Exclusion (Subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i), Regulation 2903): Outlays and expenses for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as facility rent) are excluded under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods, except for lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for a special-purpose building prescribed under section 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations (approved by the Department of Finance Canada on a building-by-building basis). Where a lease covers both a building and equipment, the claimant must make a reasonable allocation between the building (non-allowable) and the equipment (allowable). Note that structures such as bridges or hydro-electric transmission towers, as well as tents, canvas marquees, and air-supported fabric domes, are not considered "buildings" (which require walls and a roof affixed to land) and may qualify if lease rules are met.

body.text: Section 5: Government Assistance, Direct Grants, and Stacking Mechanics
5.1 Statutory Treatment of Government and Non-Government Assistance

Under paragraphs 37(1)(d) and (d.1) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, both the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or provincial super-allowance benefit amount in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year.

items: Definitions (Subsection 127(9) and Paragraph 12(1)(x)): "Government assistance" is assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (an entity with a duty to the public, subject to a significant degree of government control, that uses its profits for the benefit of the public, including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and indirect government funding channelled through non-profit organizations) whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance other than the federal SR&ED ITC. "Non-government assistance" is an amount that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)) received as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance.

Timing Rules (Sections 3.1 to 3.3, Assistance and Contract Payments Policy): A provincial or territorial R&D tax credit is considered "received" at the earliest of when it is credited to the claimant's tax instalment account, when it reduces tax payable for a taxation year, or when it is paid as a tax refund. Furthermore, a claimant can "reasonably be expected to receive" assistance if it applied for assistance and circumstances indicate it will be received, if it was advised assistance will be received, or if it earned the current year's provincial/territorial R&D tax credit and added the amount to its provincial R&D tax credit pool to be carried forward to future years (even when in a loss position, unless the claimant formally renounces the provincial tax credit where permitted).

Provincial Tax Credits Attributable to the Notional PPA: Under Sections 4.5 and 6.1 of the Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, the portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does not reduce the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (because the PPA is not included in the subsection 37(1) pool; instead, that portion of the provincial credit is included directly in business income in the year received), but it does reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures for federal ITC calculation purposes.

Non-Arm's Length Assistance Allocation (Subsection 127(20) & Form T1145): Where government or non-government assistance or a contract payment is received by one party in a non-arm's length group while another NAL party performs the SR&ED, the parties may file Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to allocate the assistance. When total assistance and contract payments relating to a project exceed the SR&ED expenditures of the project, subsection 127(19) reduces the qualified SR&ED expenditures of the claimant and NAL parties to nil.

body.text: 5.2 Stacking SR&ED with Direct Federal Innovation Grants (NRC IRAP, Clusters, SIF)

In practice, Canadian corporations stack upfront direct R&D grants with year-end SR&ED tax credits. According to industry grant data, active technology SMEs stacking NRC IRAP (National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program, which funds up to 80% of internal technical staff salaries for SMEs with ≤500 employees alongside Industrial Technology Advisor support) with SR&ED recover an average of 60% to 85% of their cash R&D costs. Other major stackable federal programs include Global Innovation Clusters (such as Scale AI, where members co-invest in cluster-led projects) and the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund (SRF) (which provides a minimum contribution of $10,000,000 for large scale-up and commercialization projects with at least $20,000,000 in eligible costs).
Crucial Stacking Mechanics Under the Proxy Method: The CRA's Worked Example

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, government assistance (such as NRC IRAP or wage subsidies like the Canada Emergency Wage Subsidy [CEWS] and Temporary Wage Subsidy [TWS]) reduces total allowable SR&ED expenditures and total qualified SR&ED expenditures, but does NOT reduce the directly engaged salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA).
The CRA's Guidance: How the Canada emergency wage subsidy affects SR&ED claims demonstrates this exact calculation on Form T661 across two employees over a 12-week period:

items: Employee 1 – Sarah (Lead Engineer): Total salary = $16,800 ($1,400/week), spending 100% of her time in directly engaged SR&ED activities. Government wage subsidy received = $10,164. Net SR&ED salary = $6,636 ($16,800 − $10,164).

Employee 2 – Jamaal (Administrative Assistant): Total salary = $8,400 ($700/week), spending 30% of his time in directly attributable (overhead support) SR&ED activities. Total SR&ED salary (30%) = $2,520. Government wage subsidy earned for SR&ED (30% of $6,300 total subsidy) = $1,890. Net SR&ED salary = $630 ($2,520 − $1,890).

cells: Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Starting Point for ITC)
Add: Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% of $16,800 Unreduced Directly Engaged Salary)
Less: Total Government Assistance for SR&ED (Sarah $10,164 + Jamaal $1,890)

body.text: As the CRA table demonstrates, because the 55% PPA ($9,240) is calculated on Sarah's gross $16,800 salary prior to subtracting the wage subsidy, electing the Proxy Method yields $13,986 in qualified SR&ED expenditures compared to $7,266 under the Traditional Method—nearly doubling the resulting federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit.

body.text: 6.2 Deep-Dive: Québec's 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul (Effective After March 25, 2025)

For taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec eliminated its legacy R&D tax credits—the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V, which Revenu Québec rejects for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, though a cumulative fee balance at the end of a taxation year ending after March 25, 2025, may continue to entitle a claimant to a credit for taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029), and the tax credit for technological adaptation services and industrial design.

In their place, Québec enacted the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (accessible online as Form RD-1029.8.CR) with the corporate income tax return alongside Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures).

items: Eligible Claimants: Only corporations (and corporations that are members of a qualified partnership) operating a business in Québec and maintaining an establishment in Québec that undertake eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec (or have them undertaken on their behalf under a contract in Québec) can claim the CRIC.
Eligible R&D and Pre-Commercialization Activities:
Eligible R&D: Harmonized with federal legislation (basic research, applied research, and experimental development, with scientific reviews conducted by the CRA).

Eligible Pre-Commercialization Activities: Must be undertaken in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation, and consist of: (a) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; (b) product design, including form and aesthetics development, improved functionality, and choice of materials; and (c) quality control activities for a product or process only if they relate to implementing a quality control system required for initial approval or certification.
Qualified Expenditures and Capital Property:
100% of salaries or wages paid to the corporation's employees;
50% of the amount paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec;
50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, an eligible research consortium, or an eligible university entity; and

Property Acquisition Costs (Capital Expenditures): Capital property acquisition costs incurred for R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec qualify, excluding costs related to acquiring a building, land, or a right to use a building or land. A corporation cannot claim both the CRIC and another Québec tax credit (such as the Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation, C3i, on Form CO-1029.8.36.II) on the same expenditure, nor can a corporation holding a Large Investment Project tax holiday certificate claim the CRIC on property used in that project.
Applicable Exclusion Threshold and Refundable Tax Credit Rates:

Qualified expenditures in a taxation year must exceed an Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of (a) $50,000 or (b) the sum of the basic personal amount of the applicable Québec personal income tax system for each employee, adjusted to reflect the time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

The CRIC is 100% refundable at a rate of 30% on the portion of qualified expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold up to a maximum of $1,000,000, and 20% on qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000 (for a corporation that is a member of a qualified partnership, the tax credit rate is 20%). Any government or non-government financial assistance must be subtracted from qualified expenditures.

body.text: 6.3 Deep-Dive: Ontario's R&D Tax Credit System (OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC)
Ontario corporations can coordinate up to three provincial R&D tax credits administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario):

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC – Schedule T2SCH566 and Schedule T2SCH31): An 8% refundable tax credit for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016 (10% prior) on up to $3,000,000 of annual qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures. The $3,000,000 expenditure limit phases out when prior-year taxable paid-up capital exceeds $25,000,000 (eliminated at $50,000,000) or when prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC – Schedules T2SCH568 and T2SCH569): Authorized under section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007, providing a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures under eligible contracts with Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs), subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC – Schedule T2SCH508): Authorized under sections 38 to 45 of the Taxation Act, 2007, providing a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016 (4.5% prior) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reconciled after OITC and OBRITC). Because a non-refundable provincial credit earned and added to the provincial credit carryforward pool is treated by the CRA as government assistance "reasonably expected to be received" that reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures in the current year unless renounced, corporations that do not wish to receive a provincial credit must formally renounce it by the filing-due date of their corporate income tax return (6 months after taxation year-end).

body.text: Section 7: Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Audit Defence
7.1 Prescribed Forms and Structural Requirements (Form T661, Schedule 31, Form T2038(IND))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025, with May 2026 form releases), a claimant must file two sets of prescribed forms containing prescribed information by the SR&ED reporting deadline: (1) Form T661 to identify SR&ED expenditures and compute the subsection 37(1) pool and subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures, and (2) Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals and trusts) to claim the Investment Tax Credit.
Structure of Form T661 (Current Version t661-26e.pdf / t661-fill-26e.pdf, Published May 15, 2026)
Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, accompanied by Guide T4088) comprises the following parts:

items: Part 1 – General Information: Claimant identification and method selection.

Part 2 – Project Information (Sections A to C): Requests technical information about the work claimed through fields, checkboxes, and questions (including Lines 270–282 for supporting evidence, and Lines 262 and 263 for entering the names of the 10 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital properties claimed on Line 390 for each project). While a separate complete Part 2 is required for each project claimed, claimants may choose to submit Part 2 with the claim for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value when filing, provided that (a) the cost of every project claimed is included in Part 6, and (b) the claimant completes and maintains at its place of business a complete Part 2 for every project claimed (failure to provide a maintained Part 2 for any project upon CRA request will result in the disallowance of the SR&ED expenditures claimed for that project). For classified projects, the claimant includes a copy of the classification letter with Form T661 and does not submit the separate sheet containing Section B of Part 2 with the return, but must retain a copy in its records.

Part 3 – Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures (Sections A to C): Computes allowable SR&ED expenditures and the subsection 37(1) pool (including Line 310 prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year, Line 360 Traditional overhead and <90% equipment lease costs, Line 390 post-December 15, 2024 depreciable capital property, Line 440 proceeds of disposition of SR&ED capital property, and Line 450 prior-year undeducted pool balance).

Part 4 – Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes: Computes total qualified SR&ED expenditures (including Line 504 for 25% First Term and 25% Second Term Shared-Use Equipment [SUE] and naming the 20 most expensive SUE properties acquired after December 15, 2024, and Line 540 for qualified expenditures transferred to a NAL payer under Form T1146).
Part 5 – Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (Sections A and B): Completed if electing the Proxy Method.
Part 6 – Project Costs: Mandatory project-by-project cost allocation for all SR&ED projects claimed in the year.
Part 7 – Additional Information: Statistical program data.
Part 8 – Claim Checklist: Filing verification checklist.

Part 9 – Claim Preparer Information: Mandatory disclosure of every claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim and their billing arrangements (if no claim preparer assisted, the claimant completes only Lines 935, 970, and 975).
Part 10 – Certification: Signed legal certification by the claimant (which cannot be revoked to withdraw a claim after it is selected for review).

body.text: Prescribed ITC Forms and Related Agreements

Claiming an ITC is not done on Form T661. Corporations must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, updated May 22, 2026), providing prescribed information in Parts 2, 3, 8 to 17, 24, and 25 (identifying in Part 12 the ITC deducted from Part I tax, carried back to previous years, or claimed as a cash refund), accompanied where applicable by Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026). Individuals, trusts (filing with the T3 Trust Income Tax and Information Return), and individual members of a partnership must file Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)), accompanied where applicable by Forms T1145, T1146, T1174, and T1263. For partnerships exempt from filing T5013 forms (such as a two-individual partnership), each individual partner must file Form T2038(IND) along with a copy of the partnership's Form T661, partnership financial statements, and schedules showing the calculation and allocation of the partnership's ITC on or before their reporting deadline. Note that under Form T1145 and Form T1146, both the transferor and transferee must file completed copies on or before the transferor's tax return filing-due date, or within the period in which the transferor (or transferee, for its first tax year ending at or after the end of the transferor's year) may serve a Notice of Objection to a Part I tax assessment.
7.2 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the Subsection 220(2.2) Bar on Extensions

Under subsection 37(11), paragraph 127(9)(m), subsection 150(1), and subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred:

items: Corporations (Paragraph 150(1)(a)): A corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year (if the tax year-end is not the last day of a month, the T2 is due on the same calendar day of the 6th month). Adding 12 months gives a corporation up to 18 months after the end of the taxation year (determined by calendar months rather than a day count) to file or amend Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31. For example, a March 31, 2022 tax year-end has a T2 filing-due date of September 30, 2022, and an SR&ED reporting deadline of September 30, 2023; a February 28 tax year-end has a T2 due date of August 31 and an SR&ED reporting deadline of August 31 of the following year; and a January 6 tax year-end has a T2 due date of July 6 and an SR&ED reporting deadline of July 6 of the following year.

Individuals Carrying on a Business (Subparagraph 150(1)(d)(ii)): An individual's tax year is the calendar year (December 31), with a T1 filing-due date of June 15 of the following year. Adding 12 months gives an individual 17.5 months after the end of the tax year (until June 15 of the second following year; e.g., June 15, 2025, for the December 31, 2023 tax year) to file or amend Form T661 and Form T2038(IND).

Trusts (Paragraph 150(1)(c)): A trust's T3 filing-due date is 90 days after the end of its taxation year. Adding 12 months gives a trust 90 days plus 12 months (approximately 15 months) after the end of its taxation year (e.g., for a December 31, 2023 trust year-end, the T3 due date is March 30, 2024, and the SR&ED reporting deadline is March 30, 2025).

Non-Profit SR&ED Corporations: Cannot claim an ITC; their reporting deadline for deducting expenditures on Form T661 is their corporate income tax return filing-due date (up to 6 months after tax year-end).

body.text: If an SR&ED reporting deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or a CRA-recognized public holiday, the claim is considered filed on time if received by the CRA or postmarked on or before the next business day. Furthermore, all corporations with annual gross revenue of more than $1,000,000 must file their T2 return electronically (with limited exceptions), and any electronic amendment to Form T661 or Schedule T2SCH31 must be transmitted with an amended tax return for the year.
Consequences of Missing the Reporting Deadline and Subsection 220(2.2)

items: Filing Form T661 Without Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND): If Form T661 containing prescribed information is filed by the SR&ED reporting deadline, but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the reporting deadline, the claimant may still deduct the allowable SR&ED expenditures from income or include them in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, but the claimant is permanently barred from earning any ITC on those expenditures.

Filing Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND) Without Form T661: If Form T661 is not filed containing the prescribed expenditure information by the SR&ED reporting deadline (subsection 37(11.1)), the expenditures are not considered to be SR&ED expenditures, no deduction is allowed, and no ITC is earned.

Deficiencies and Partial Claims: If a claim is filed before the reporting deadline with missing prescribed information, the CRA cannot grant any extension past the statutory reporting deadline to cure the deficiency. However, if a claimant claims 15 projects on Form T661 and submits Part 2 project information on time for 10 projects while omitting Part 2 for 5 projects, the CRA will not disallow the entire claim: the 10 compliant projects are accepted, while the 5 deficient projects are disallowed.

No Ministerial Waiver (Subsection 220(2.2)): Under subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act (applicable on or after November 17, 2005), requests to waive or extend the filing requirements of subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) under the Minister's general fairness power in subsection 220(2.1) cannot be made.

body.text: 7.3 Penalties: Part 9 Preparer Penalties and Subsection 163(2) Gross Negligence Penalties
Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty ($1,000 Joint and Several Liability)

Claim preparer information in Part 9 of Form T661 is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline, and an SR&ED claim will not be disallowed if Part 9 is the only missing, incomplete, or inaccurate information filed. However, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed if the prescribed information regarding claim preparers and billing arrangements in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, and where a claim preparer prepared or assisted in preparing the form, both the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable for the $1,000 penalty.
Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2) ITA)

Under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), a civil penalty applies to any person who knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes, participates in, agrees to, or accepts a false statement or omission in an original or amended income tax return or SR&ED claim. The burden of proof lies on the CRA to establish on a balance of probabilities that the false statement or omission resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the rules.

The penalty equals the greater of $100 or 50% of the understated Part I tax payable (and/or overstated refundable ITC refund) reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission. When calculating the penalty, the CRA applies a strict "First-Deducted Assumption" ordering rule: overstated amounts are treated as being deducted first from the subsection 37(1) pool and against Part I tax payable before considering legitimate SR&ED expenditures or prior-year balances, and a claimant cannot offset the penalty calculation by requesting an additional deduction such as unclaimed Capital Cost Allowance (CCA).
The CRA's policy provides two comprehensive penalty calculation examples:

items: Example 1 – Understated Income & Part I Tax Payable (15% Basic ITC Rate): A claimant files $600,000 in allowable SR&ED expenditures (revised by CRA to $500,000 = $100,000 overstated), with $165,000 PPA (no change), yielding $765,000 filed vs. $665,000 revised qualified expenditures ($100,000 overstated) and an overstated 15% ITC of $15,000. Taking the $600,000 pool deduction understated taxable income by $100,000 and understated Part I tax (at 20%) by $20,000, while deducting the overstated ITC understated Part I tax by an additional $15,000, for a total understated Part I tax payable of $35,000 ($20,000 + $15,000). The 50% gross negligence penalty is $17,500 (50% of $35,000), and requesting $100,000 of available CCA to offset net income does not reduce the $17,500 penalty.

Example 2 – Understated Part I Tax Payable with PPA Amplification (35% Enhanced ITC Rate): A CCPC knowingly or with gross negligence claims $400,000 of directly engaged SR&ED salaries (revised by CRA to $200,000 = $200,000 overstated) and $240,000 of materials consumed (revised to $220,000 = $20,000 overstated), overstating total allowable SR&ED expenditures by $220,000 ($640,000 claimed vs. $420,000 revised). Because the 55% PPA is calculated on salaries, the PPA is also overstated by $110,000 ($220,000 claimed vs. $110,000 revised), causing total qualified SR&ED expenditures to be overstated by $330,000 ($860,000 claimed vs. $530,000 revised) and the 35% enhanced ITC to be overstated by $115,500 ($301,000 claimed vs. $185,500 revised), triggering a gross negligence penalty on the resulting $115,500 understatement of Part I tax payable ($19,000 filed vs. $134,500 revised).

body.text: 7.4 CRA Review Process, Service Standards, Pre-Claim Approval, and Dispute Resolution

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026) and Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (updated December 5, 2025), all SR&ED claims undergo risk assessment (incorporating increased AI risk screening implemented April 1, 2026, to avoid subjecting low-risk claims to unnecessary audit interventions). Once a claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn because Form T661 is part of the income tax return and the Part 10 certification cannot be revoked.

items: CRA Service Standards:
Refundable Claims Selected for Review: 180 calendar days from the date the CRA receives a complete claim (targeted 90% of the time).

Elective Pre-Claim Approval Projects (Implemented April 1, 2026): Provides businesses with upfront technical approval of eligible SR&ED projects; for pre-approved claims requiring an expenditure-only review, processing time is cut in half to 90 calendar days (unless projects differ significantly from what was approved or include non-approved projects).
Non-Refundable Claims: No service standard processing time.

Review Execution and Outside Consultant Conflict Rules: Reviews are conducted by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) for technical eligibility and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]) for expenditure allowability. Most reviews are conducted virtually via videoconferencing (though an on-site visit may be requested on an exceptional case-by-case basis), and files may be assigned across time zones under the National File Assignment System (with meetings scheduled during the claimant's local business hours). Oral interview statements supplement, but do not replace, contemporaneous written documentation. Under Application Policy SR&ED 95-04R (Conflict of Interest with Regard to Outside Consultants, issued by Jim Millen, Director, Specialized Compliance Enhancement Division), if the CRA retains an outside consultant to advise on technical eligibility, that consultant must declare any conflict of interest prior to the review, must never concurrently prepare SR&ED claims or offer income tax/SR&ED advice to taxpayers, must have their curriculum vitae (CV) shown to the taxpayer upon request, and must be replaced if a real or potential conflict of interest is demonstrated (with unresolved issues escalated to the Senior Science Advisor in Headquarters).
Three-Step Administrative Dispute Resolution and Formal Appeals:
Step 1: Discuss concerns directly with the RTA and/or FR.
Step 2: Escalate to the RTM and/or FRM to review the facts and perspectives.

Step 3 – Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the CRA's 30-day proposal package and before the file is closed by reviewers, the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Canada Revenue Agency, Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5), which forwards the request within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director. An Administrative Review is not a second technical review; rather, the Assistant Director (or delegate) evaluates whether the technical and financial reviews were consistent with SR&ED legislation and policies and whether the claimant received due process (reasonable opportunity and time to explain work and submit additional information, clear requests for clarification, consideration of all submitted information, and a clear eligibility report and expenditure disallowance explanation).

Formal Appeals: Once the review is finalized and a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, a claimant that disagrees with the findings may file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: Section 8: Foundational Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents
Canadian SR&ED tax administration is governed by binding case law from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
8.1 Summary Table of Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence

headers: Judicial Holding & Precedential Impact on SR&ED Audits

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC)
Tax Court of Canada (1998, per Justice Bowman)
Statutory interpretation of "scientific research and experimental development" under subsection 248(1) ITA.

Established the foundational Five Criteria for SR&ED eligibility (at para. 16); confirmed that Information Circular 86-4R3 was a useful and reliable guide (at para. 15); held that slight or incremental technological advancements qualify.
Appellate endorsement of Northwest Hydraulic and evidentiary burden for repeatable testing.

Approved Justice Bowman's five Northwest Hydraulic criteria at the appellate level (at para. 10) and held that taxpayers must produce reliable evidence of actual testing data and repeatable experimental evaluation.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740, [2001] FCJ No. 1886
Federal Court of Appeal (2001, per Justice Sexton for Stone, Evans, and Sexton JJ.)
Appellate codification of the five-question test for SR&ED eligibility.

Unanimously summarized and affirmed the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria (at para. 17) as the governing legal standard across Canada; confirmed that "technological uncertainty" (not merely "technical uncertainty") is the proper legal standard.
Tax Court of Canada & Federal Court of Appeal
Boundary between routine engineering / product improvement and experimental development.

Held that where a claimant's objective is to improve an existing product using known engineering methods without resolving an underlying technological uncertainty (paras. 10, 16, 17, 22, 28), the work does not qualify as SR&ED.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313
Tax Court of Canada (Oct 23, 2014, per Justice Gaston Jorré)
Whether contemporaneous documentation is a mandatory legal condition (sine qua non) for SR&ED eligibility, and impartiality of CRA expert witnesses.

Allowed the taxpayer's appeal: held that while contemporaneous documents are relevant to proving questions of fact, the existence of contemporaneous documentation is NOT a legal condition for SR&ED to be recognized. Criticized the Crown's expert witness (Mr. Kooi) for confusing his audit role as a CRA scientific adviser guided by CRA policies with his duty of independent expertise as a court expert.
Role of contemporaneous documentation under the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion.

Confirmed (at para. 118, alongside Les Abeilles) that a detailed contemporaneous record is not explicitly required by the Income Tax Act or Regulations as a statutory condition, though the taxpayer must still prove a systematic investigation.
Joel Theatrical Rigging (JTR) Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6
Quantitative experimental measurement required to satisfy the scientific method.

Upheld the CRA's denial of SR&ED claims; held that had the claimant followed a systematic experimental process, its personnel (Mr. Marineau and colleagues) would have precisely measured the weights used and the exact duration of descent in each experiment to determine whether descent duration was increasing or decreasing across sequential tests.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88
Whether adherence to the "scientific method" is legally required when the words "scientific method" do not appear in subsection 248(1) ITA.

Dismissed the taxpayer's appeal; rejected the argument that the "scientific method" criterion should not apply because the words are absent from subsection 248(1), reaffirming that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the settled judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1).
Federal Court of Appeal (May 2022, per Justice Rennie)
Sufficiency of vague project timelines and applicability of the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion.

Dismissed the consulting firm's appeal; reaffirmed Kam-Press and Northwest Hydraulic, holding that the taxpayer's records (a "Project Timeline" presented by Mr. Saini on the "PTS Project") were "vague," "unclear," and failed to show a "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests".
Eligibility of food manufacturing R&D (developing custom frozen pie recipes across 2013–2016).

Ruled in favour of the appellant food manufacturer across denied projects from 2013 to 2016 (totalling $343,449 in denied expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs excluding 2014); held that the evidence of CEO Mr. Pandya satisfied the Northwest Hydraulic criteria for developing and testing custom frozen pie recipes.
Whether contemporaneous timesheets are mandatory to substantiate SR&ED work.

Held (at para. 119) that although the CRA would have liked to see contemporaneous timesheets for the work performed, contemporaneous timesheets are not necessarily required for work to be eligible as qualifying SR&ED.
David Ludmer et al. and Ludco Enterprises Ltd. v. MNR, 93 DTC 1351 at 1423; The Queen v. McKinley Transport Ltd., 90 DTC 6243; AGT Ltd. v. Canada, 97 DTC 5189
Supreme Court / Federal Court of Appeal
Scope of CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) audit authority and document relevance.

Cited in the CRA Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors: Ludmer confirms the CRA's authority to expand a review to additional projects or issues not originally identified in the review plan; McKinley Transport and AGT Ltd. confirm that the relevance of requested documents can often only be determined after the RTA has had the opportunity to inspect and review them.

body.text: 8.2 Detailed Synthesis of Judicial Principles for Audit Defence
The Five Northwest Hydraulic / C.W. Agencies Criteria in Modern Litigation

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 at para. 16), Justice Bowman laid down five criteria—subsequently approved and summarized by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087 at para. 10) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393 at para. 17)—that govern judicial determination of whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1):

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? The work must seek to generate information that advances our understanding of scientific relations or technologies and advances the taxpayer's technological knowledge base.
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?

Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), taxpayers argued that because subsection 248(1) (and the CRA's revised 2021 guidelines) refers to a "systematic investigation or search" rather than the "scientific method," the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion should not apply. The Federal Court of Appeal flatly rejected this argument in both cases, holding that Northwest Hydraulic remains the settled legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) and requires methodical testing with precise measurement (as in Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6) and a logical progression between the premise of each experiment and its result.
Did the process result in a technological advancement? As recognized in Northwest Hydraulic, the technological advancement achieved only has to be slight in order to qualify as such.

Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed? While Justice Bowman noted in Northwest Hydraulic (at para. 16) that a detailed record of hypotheses, tests, and results should be kept as the work progresses, the Tax Court of Canada clarified in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313), Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 42 at para. 118), and DAZZM Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 129 at para. 119) that neither the Income Tax Act nor the Income Tax Regulations explicitly require contemporaneous documentation or contemporaneous timesheets as a legal condition (sine qua non) for SR&ED recognition. Rather, the existence and content of contemporaneous documents are relevant to proving questions of fact, and credible witness testimony combined with other evidence can establish eligibility (as in Les Abeilles, Canafric Inc., and DAZZM Inc.), whereas vague or retroactive records that fail to show a logical experimental progression will result in dismissal (as in National R&D Inc.).

body.text: Scope of CRA Review Authority and Expert Witness Neutrality
During an SR&ED review, the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors relies on three judicial authorities regarding audit scope and document demands:

items: David Ludmer, Brian Ludmer, Cindy Ludmer and Ludco Enterprises Ltd. v. MNR (93 DTC 1351 at 1423) confirms the authority of CRA officials to expand or diminish the scope of a review depending on the facts determined and information provided during the review process, including reviewing additional projects or issues not originally identified in the review plan or initial communications.

The Queen v. McKinley Transport Ltd. (90 DTC 6243) and AGT Ltd. v. Canada (97 DTC 5189) establish that the relevance of documents requested by an RTA is often difficult to determine until the RTA has had an actual opportunity to inspect and review them.

Conversely, in litigation before the Tax Court of Canada, Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313) establishes a strict boundary between a CRA scientific adviser's audit role and their role as an expert witness in court: while a CRA adviser at the audit stage is naturally guided by CRA guidelines and evidentiary standards, an expert witness in court must provide an independent opinion grounded in their personal scientific expertise rather than applying CRA administrative guidelines.

body.text: Section 9: Comprehensive Verification Checklist for Canadian SR&ED Claimants (2025–2026 Taxation Years)

To ensure full statutory compliance and maximize combined federal and provincial recoveries under the post-December 15, 2024 (Bill C-15) and post-March 25, 2025 (Québec CRIC) regimes, corporate tax directors and R&D auditors should execute the following verification protocol prior to filing:

items: Confirm Taxation Year Cutoffs for Bill C-15 Enhancements: Verify whether the corporation's taxation year begins after December 15, 2024, to apply the doubled $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the broadened $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out thresholds, and Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) eligibility for the 35% enhanced refundable ITC.

Evaluate the CCPC Revenue Election vs. Taxable Capital Method: For CCPCs (or associated CCPC groups) whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, model whether making the election under subsection 127(10.31) (or the joint election under subsection 127(10.32) for associated CCPCs) to calculate the $6,000,000 expenditure limit using the 3-year average annual revenue method preserves a higher enhanced 35% expenditure limit.

Capture Restored Post-December 15, 2024 Capital, SUE, and Lease Expenditures: Identify all new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, intended for ≥90% (ASA) SR&ED operating time or value consumption to claim 100% on Line 390 of Form T661 (and list the 10 most expensive properties per project on Lines 262 and 263); identify new multi-use equipment (>50% to <90% SR&ED use, excluding GPOEF and Regulation 2900(11) Prescribed Depreciable Property) to claim 25% First Term SUE and 25% Second Term SUE on Line 504 (listing the 20 most expensive SUE items); and claim post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs (100% if ≥90% ASA; 50% under Proxy if >50% to <90% excluding GPOEF; or proportional SR&ED percentage on Line 360 under Traditional).

Enforce the 180-Day Payment Cutoffs: Audit all accrued SR&ED salaries/wages and current vendor/subcontractor payables before the 180th day following taxation year-end so that unpaid remuneration is not disqualified from both the pool and ITCs under subsection 78(4), unpaid current expenses are not deferred for ITCs under subsection 127(26), and non-arm's length transfers on Form T1146 (subsection 127(13)) are not permanently forfeited.

Validate Specified Employee Caps and Form T1174: Exclude all bonuses and remuneration based on profits for specified employees (subsection 37(9)), cap their subsection 37(1) pool salary at 5 × YMPE, cap their Proxy salary base at the lesser of 75% of eligible salary or 2.5 × YMPE (Regulation 2900(7)), and file Form T1174 accompanied by a certified Directors' resolution (or sole-shareholder confirmation) before the SR&ED reporting deadline if any specified employee worked for two or more associated corporations.

Transition Québec Claims to the CRIC Regime: For Québec taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, retire legacy Form RD-1029.7-V and file Form RD-1029.8.CR-T / RD-1029.8.CR (with Form RD-222-V) to claim the 30% / 20% refundable CRIC across eligible R&D, pre-commercialization activities (regulatory validations/studies, product design, and initial certification quality control systems), and capital property acquisitions above the $50,000 / employee basic-personal-amount exclusion threshold.

Lock In the 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline: Calendar the exact calendar-month date 18 months after the corporate taxation year-end (or 17.5 months for individuals / 15 months for trusts) to submit Form T661 (including Part 9 preparer disclosure to avoid the $1,000 joint-and-several penalty), Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND), Schedule T2SCH49, Form T1145, Form T1146, Form T1174, Form T1263, and all provincial schedules (renouncing non-refundable provincial credits like the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC within 6 months of year-end if in a loss position), recognizing that subsection 220(2.2) prohibits any ministerial extension or waiver of the SR&ED reporting deadline.
